debate.situation: You have an offer paying 25% more, but it adds 90 minutes of commuting each way, and you want to know if it is worth it. What you have reported is the raise and the commute; everything else is unknown. The decisive unknowns are how many days you would actually travel, whether you would drive or ride a train, and what the extra money would do for you. The question may also be wider than yes or no, since terms like remote days or a counteroffer might be possible.

minds.title: The Market Economist
minds.concern: Every job is an exchange, and the question is whether the pay fairly compensates for what the job costs you in time and comfort.
minds.author: Adam Smith

minds.title: The Forecasting Skeptic
minds.concern: People predict badly how a change will feel day to day, so the decision should not rest on a vivid number or a guess about adjustment.
minds.author: Daniel Kahneman

minds.title: The Time Accountant
minds.concern: Hours are the one resource you cannot earn back, so every choice is a trade of finite life, not just a budget line.
minds.author: Oliver Burkeman

debate.speaker: The Market Economist
debate.text: Start with arithmetic. Assume five office days and a forty-hour week. Three commuting hours a day adds fifteen weekly hours, so you tie up fifty-five hours for twenty-five percent more money. Per hour, that is roughly a nine percent pay cut. Unpleasant work should be paid extra, and this raise may not clear that bar.
debate.author: Adam Smith
debate.basis: Basis: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations

debate.speaker: The Forecasting Skeptic
debate.text: Your sum looks solid but rests on guesses. The raise is a crisp number, so it looms large; the daily grind is vague, so it shrinks. People judge a change by whichever feature they are staring at. Counting a commute hour exactly like a work hour is also just an assumption.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.speaker: The Time Accountant
debate.text: You are both haggling over the exchange rate. I would ask what those fifteen hours are for. Money converts into almost anything except time. And do not hunt for the option with no loss; every yes here is a no to something, and the honest question is which loss you can live with.
debate.author: Oliver Burkeman
debate.basis: Basis: Oliver Burkeman, Four Thousand Weeks

debate.speaker: The Market Economist
debate.text: Fair hit on my assumptions, so let me make them testable. Commute hours need not count as fully as work hours. The break-even is when a commute hour feels two thirds as bad as a work hour. Below that, the raise wins; above it, you lose. Which side are you on? Nobody can say from the armchair.
debate.author: Adam Smith
debate.basis: Basis: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations

debate.speaker: The Forecasting Skeptic
debate.text: Then the missing fact is how you would travel and how often. If you would go in only two or three days, or ride a train where you can read, the break-even is easy to clear. If it is five days of driving, it is very hard. I would price those cases separately, not average them.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.speaker: The Time Accountant
debate.text: Careful with the train. Turning a commute into reading time is how people convince themselves a bad trade is fine. Even a pleasant three hours takes the edges off every day. The cost is not only the hours but the shape: mornings and evenings are the only free time most people have.
debate.author: Oliver Burkeman
debate.basis: Basis: Oliver Burkeman, Four Thousand Weeks

debate.speaker: The Market Economist
debate.text: Then I will name the conflict instead of settling it. More money and more time pull in opposite directions, and only you can rank them. I would go further than Smith here: the extra money matters more if it relieves real pressure, such as debt or a savings gap, and less if you are already comfortable.
debate.author: Adam Smith
debate.basis: Basis: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations

debate.speaker: The Forecasting Skeptic
debate.text: Use that against the raise: if comfort is the question, the number matters less than what it buys. And the motive may differ from the stated question. You might want the raise for security, or want out of the current job, or feel pressure from others who call it a no-brainer. Each calls for a different move, including negotiating remote days.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.speaker: The Time Accountant
debate.text: I will take negotiation, with a warning. Waiting for a perfect version is its own trap, because eventually something is sacrificed. As for motive, I suspect security more than escape, but I cannot know. Notice that nobody has asked about the new job itself. A better role could outweigh the commute.
debate.author: Oliver Burkeman
debate.basis: Basis: Oliver Burkeman, Four Thousand Weeks

debate.speaker: The Forecasting Skeptic
debate.text: Good, then test instead of guessing. Do the real route at real rush hour for a week and rate each day. A trial week has a flaw, since novelty may hide the grind. I would go further than Kahneman: as I recall, long, tiring commutes are one thing people tend not to get used to. That is my hunch, not his claim.
debate.author: Daniel Kahneman
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow

debate.speaker: The Market Economist
debate.text: I accept the trial and keep my point: a price exists. If a week of rush hours leaves you drained, then twenty-five percent is too cheap. If you barely notice, it is a good deal. The Accountant still thinks no price buys back the evenings. That disagreement is real and belongs to you.
debate.author: Adam Smith
debate.basis: Basis: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations

debate.clearer: The main insight is that the decision turns less on the headline raise than on two things: how bad a commute hour feels to you, and how many such hours you would really face. On the stated assumptions, a five-day schedule makes the raise roughly break even if a commute hour feels about two thirds as bad as a work hour, and remote days change that quickly. Still disputed is whether hours should be priced at all, since the Time Accountant sees the loss of evenings as more than a rate. A possible self-reflection: is the pull toward this offer about the money, security, leaving the current job, or the new role?
debate.dependsOn: If you would travel only some days, or can negotiate remote days: the raise becomes more reasonable, because the added hours shrink while the pay stays. If it is five days, mostly driving, and the extra money is not relieving real pressure: declining or countering becomes more reasonable, because you would trade a large block of free time for a modest gain. If the new role itself is clearly better, that can outweigh part of the commute cost, though it does not erase it. If the key unknown is how a commute hour would feel to you: do a trial week of the actual route at actual times, rating each day, and check what the extra money would actually change in your finances.
